What is the essential teaching in 'An Heir to the Dhamma'?

In 'An Heir to the Dhamma', the teaching opens with this observation: *"A talk given to the monks at Wat Pa Baan Taad."* The central invitation is to turn one's investigation inward — to verify the Dhamma not as a set of beliefs, but as directly observable reality in one's own body, speech, and mind. As the text teaches, the Dhamma is *akāliko* — ever-present — and *opanayiko* — leading inward — available to be known (*paccattaṁ*) by each practitioner for themselves. There is no need to search elsewhere; the truth is already here.

The teaching explains: *"A talk given to the monks at Wat Pa Baan Taad.
The ordinary mind—no matter whose—when it doesn’t yet have any standards and meets up with things that drag it here and there in the wrong directions, will tend to go rolling after those preoccupations without let-up, to the point where it can’t find an..."* 'Listening to the Dhamma at all times' (sato sampajāno) means using every sensory encounter as an object of mindful investigation. The eye sees form — note impermanence. The ear hears sound — note how it arises and passes. The mind encounters a thought — note how it dissolves without being held. Every moment is a Dhamma talk being given by reality itself. The practitioner's task is to stay awake, curious, and non-reactive — receiving the continuous teaching without grasping or rejecting.
